strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 20+ diverse tasks (MuJoCo, ManiSkill state/RGB) with consistent improvements (1.3-1.9x sample efficiency gains on several tasks) and proper statistical reporting (5 seeds, 95% confidence intervals)

Solid theoretical contribution: Proposition 4.1 rigorously analyzes gradient variance differences between Gaussian and categorical policies with tight bounds; provides useful intuition despite simplified toy setting

Thorough ablation studies effectively isolate design choices: loss-swap ablation (Figure 6b) elegantly shows cross-entropy vs squared error is critical, component analysis validates each architectural choice, and bin granularity sweep reveals sensitivity

Clear presentation and well-motivated approach: The paper articulates compelling analogy between cross-entropy success in value learning and its application to policy optimization; writing is accessible and logical flow is strong

Strong reproducibility: Comprehensive hyperparameters (Table 1), detailed environment specifications (Appendix B.2), complete learning curves, and use of established codebases (CleanRL, ManiSkill) enable easy reproduction

Principled experimental design: Fair comparisons with identical critic architecture across variants; systematic component analysis showing residual connections and layer norm each contribute independently
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: Discretized categorical policies already explored by Tang & Agrawal (2020) and Zhu et al. (2024); regularized architectures (residual blocks with layer norm) are standard in modern ML and prior RL work (SimBa, BroNet). Main contribution is demonstrating their combination works well—an engineering contribution more than a fundamental algorithmic advance

Narrow algorithmic scope: All experiments use PPO only with no evaluation of other on-policy methods (TRPO, A3C, A2C, newer variants), limiting generalizability of findings despite claims of contributing to 'on-policy RL' broadly

Incomplete mechanistic understanding: Proposition 4.1 assumes constant return and vanilla REINFORCE, yet realistic PPO uses advantage baselines, clipping, and GAE normalization—applicability gap remains unclear. Missing analysis of why regularization specifically helps categorical policies or their interaction

Lack of principled hyperparameter guidance: Performance highly sensitive to bin count (Figure 6d) with substantial degradation beyond optimal K; no principled method for selecting K across task types or action dimensionalities. K=41 choice appears arbitrary and task-dependent

Oversimplified cross-entropy analysis (Section 4.2): Comparison assumes fixed Σ = σ²I for Gaussian, but many implementations learn variance; doesn't explain why cross-entropy specifically improves optimization beyond variance reduction; lacks bias-variance tradeoff discussion between discretization and continuous approximation

Mixed performance vs. strong baselines and statistical concerns: Wall-clock comparisons vs TD3/TD-MPC2 show inconsistent advantages (outperforms on StackCube but less efficient on Humanoid); some improvements have overlapping confidence intervals (e.g., HalfCheetah) without explicit significance testing

Limited analysis of failure modes and real-world applicability: No discussion of when discretized categorical policies are inappropriate (very high-dimensional actions, continuous fine-grained control), computational overhead, or guidance for scaling to different action spaces; all tasks are simulated benchmarks

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across diverse benchmarks (Gym locomotion, ManiSkill state/vision), algorithms (PPO, TRPO, SPO), with consistent improvements of 1.3-1.9× sample efficiency
Well-designed ablations, particularly the loss-swap ablation isolating the role of cross-entropy vs. squared-error objectives, showing discretization alone is insufficient
Clear motivation connecting on-policy actor updates to classification-style objectives with rigorous gradient variance analysis (Proposition 4.1) showing categorical policies have lower variance
Algorithm-agnostic generality: consistent improvements across three different on-policy algorithms demonstrates robustness
Strong reproducibility practices including promised code release, complete hyperparameter specifications, 5 random seeds with bootstrap confidence intervals, and extensive appendices
Practical value with meaningful sample efficiency gains and no runtime overhead (Table 1), making this an actionable drop-in replacement
Thorough extended studies including scaling analysis (actor width, bin count), runtime analysis, gradient signal-to-noise ratio analysis showing strong correlation with performance
weaknesses: Limited novelty: combines three existing techniques (discrete categorical policies from Tang & Agrawal 2020; regularized MLPs from SimBa/BroNet; cross-entropy loss comparison from distributional RL) without introducing fundamentally new methods
Modest theoretical contributions: Proposition 4.1 is correct but relatively straightforward, following directly from basic probability without deeper insights into optimization implications
Mixed results for vision-based tasks: performance improvements are notably smaller for RGB-based ManiSkill tasks (Figure 4), suggesting the benefits may be domain-specific

Sensitivity to discretization granularity: performance degrades sharply with large K values (Figure 8d), introducing a new hyperparameter to tune and contradicting claims of being a simple drop-in replacement
Limited experimental scope: only continuous control on standard benchmarks, no high-dimensional action spaces (>20D), and only state/pixel observations; generalization unclear
Actor-critic interaction unexplored: critic kept fixed by design, preventing understanding of joint scaling or complementary architectural choices
Hyperparameter sensitivity concern: while using defaults aids reproducibility, PPO is known to be hyperparameter-sensitive; unclear if improvements hold under task-specific tuning
Claim of 'state-of-the-art within on-policy RL' is somewhat overstated; limited comparison to other on-policy methods and performance advantage over TD3 is mixed (Appendix C.1)
